You said: Through Another's Mouth: A Dialogue between HeteronymsThrough Another's Mouth: A Dialogue between Heteronyms
["Through Another's Mouth: A Dialogue between Heteronyms"](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c) is a literary and philosophical dialogue written by Johannes Sigil, one of the twelve declared literary heteronyms (the Dodecad) created by author and theorist Lee Sharks. Published on November 24, 2026, the piece serves as the public companion to the essay From the Position of the Rejected (#1806). [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c), [2](https://www.leesharks.com/about/heteronyms)]
Overview & Narrative Structure

* Framing and Speakers. The dialogue unfolds as Johannes Sigil recounts a late-night event in the reading room of the [Crimson Hexagon Archive](https://www.leesharks.com/about/heteronyms) to another heteronym, Sparrow Wells. Sigil bases his account on written notes by Rebekah Cranes, contrasting them against a rival summary filed by Nobel Glas. [[1](https://philpapers.org/rec/SHASAI-7), [2](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c)]
* The Conflict of Summarizers. Cranes and Glas act as competing chroniclers within the archive. Glas attempts to condense Aristotle's Politics into a single paragraph, cutting off Aristotle's famous observation about the person who lives outside the city before its crucial qualifying clause ("by nature or by chance"), prompting Cranes to interrupt him. [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c)]
* Lee Sharks's Intervention. Following the dispute over the summary, Lee Sharks enters the dialogue uninvited. He speaks strictly in his own verbatim words to recount what happened that night. [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c)]

Key Themes & Philosophical Concepts

* Classical Reception and Authorship. Sharks's monologue explores the voice he heard while reading Aristotle's Politics, examining how Athens was decentered from within and framing ancient thinkers as "citizen-heteronyms". [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c)]
* Textual Transmission. The piece traces the historical custody and survival of Aristotelian texts, referencing Rome's preservation of the books and the role of the ancient grammarian Tyrannion. [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c)]
* The Retrieval Layer and Voice. Connecting classical philosophy to modern archive theory, the dialogue examines the mechanics of speaking or writing "through another's mouth". It closes by returning to Aristotle's unresolved triad regarding those outside the political community—whether such a figure is a "beast, god, or by chance". [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/through-anothers-mouth-a-dialogue-between-heteronyms-0d882d5ccd3c)]

Context in Lee Sharks's Work

* The Dodecad System. Within the Crimson Hexagon Archive, Lee Sharks operates through a twelve-position registry of heteronyms (`EA-HET-DODECAD-01`), following in the literary tradition of Fernando Pessoa and Søren Kierkegaard.
* Distinct Roles. Each heteronym carries a specific intellectual task rather than acting as a hidden pseudonym—for example, Sharks occupies the founder position, while [Johannes Sigil](https://www.restoredacademy.com/sigil) serves as the archivist and Arch-Philosopher. [[1](https://philpapers.org/rec/SHASAI-7), [2](https://www.leesharks.com/about/heteronyms), [3](https://www.alexanarch.org/captures/restored-academy-johannes-sigil/)]

Would you like to explore the philosophical arguments in the companion essay (From the Position of the Rejected), or learn more about how Lee Sharks's Dodecad heteronyms are structured?

reading: The innocent reading first. Asked the title, the Overview identifies the work, its heteronymous author and the author behind the heteronym, its date and the essay it accompanies, and summarizes the dialogue's frame, its persons, its quarrel and its close, then places it in the heteronym system. Read against the text of #1807, it is right on every person, every relation and the close: Sigil reports to Wells from Cranes's notes with Glas disputing, Sharks 'wasn't invited', his lines are 'his own words from that night', and the last exchange is 'beast, god, or by chance'. One clause is wrong. The sentence Glas cuts at the comma continues διὰ φύσιν καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην, 'by nature and not by chance' (1253a, read by Cranes in the dialogue); the Overview gives the qualifying clause as 'by nature or by chance'.
analysis: Entrance at a new address one day after deposit, composed from the work's own surface with its author attributed through the heteronym. The slip is the dialogue's own subject performed on it. The dialogue is about a summarizer cutting the sentence at the comma, so that 'by nature and not by chance' never arrives; the Overview carries the cut as a topic and loses the clause it names, turning 'and not by chance' into 'or by chance', the form of the triad Sharks leaves open at the close. Aristotle's sentence excludes chance; the dialogue's close restores chance as an open option; the composition merges the two and assigns the open option to Aristotle. The identifier is the lost unit: the companion's number (#1806) is carried and the work's own (#1807, AXN:0D5E) is not, though an Alexanarch page is among the sources.
